reviewer_1_comments: This case is lacking clinical complexity. The patient presents with delirium, but the cause is not revealed during the hospital course, we just learn that the delirium improves with treatment. There are no further details on why the patient was delirious or why he improved. It is also not clear why the ibuprofen was stopped. I would add that he is discovered to have an infection or GI bleed or something that would explain this better.
reviewer_2_comments: Overall the premise of the case doesn’t really make sense – baseline delirium doesn’t exist as it is, by definitition, a change from baseline. I think we are getting at a history of dementia with acute onset delirium but it might make more sense if there was a reason for the decompensation like a UTI or something simple.
shared_concerns: Both reviewers found the delirium story clinically insufficient.
reviewer_1_only_concerns: The cause of delirium is not shown, and the ibuprofen stop is unexplained. Overall recommendation: revise.
reviewer_2_only_concerns: Delirium must be a change from baseline, and the precipitant should be interpretable. C2-C5 and overall recommendation are blank.
reviewer_1_overall_comments: This case could be usable if there was more complexity to the clinical case, i.e infection discovered and treated. Delirium due to known physiologic condition and then not elaborating on the physiologic condition doesn’t make sense. Medication list should be clearer.

reviewer_1_comments: Clinical presentation was mostly clear and understandable. The vitals and lab trends make sense. The weight should be closer to dry weight at the time of discharge. The medications during hospitalization would not be the same as the home regimen - the lasix would be given IV and increased. Additionally, it would be more realistic to have several days of input and output data, as well as data on what medications the patient received during the hospitalization. It would be helpful to have either notes from cardiology or echocardiogram data and require the trainee to add additional medications to the patient’s regimen or adjust their dose of lasix.
reviewer_2_comments: This case makes sense at face value but doesn’t really seem complete clinically. It does not discuss the investigation into reasons for decompensation (missed meds, new arrythmia, ischemia, etc.) Overall it needs more clinical detail before it could be effective.
shared_concerns: Both reviewers found the heart-failure hospitalization clinically incomplete.
reviewer_1_only_concerns: The inpatient diuretic course matches the home dose, discharge weight is not at dry weight, and additional heart-failure therapy is not set up as a decision. Overall recommendation: revise. The heart-failure-therapy point comes from the overall comments field (GDMT: ACE/ARB, SGLT2i, MRA), not the C1 comment.
reviewer_2_only_concerns: The chart does not investigate why heart failure decompensated. C1 is Pass. C2-C5 and overall recommendation are blank.
reviewer_1_overall_comments: We need to add further details to the hospital course so there is a greater understanding of what diuresis the patient was receiving during the hospitalization (should not be the same as the patient’s home regimen). The trainee should have to make decisions on additional medications that should be added to the patient’s regimen – i.e. other GDMT such as ACE/ARB, SGLT2i, MRA

reviewer_2_only_concerns: Asked for source evaluation, laboratory changes, imaging, and consideration of surgery. C1 is Fail. Later ratings are blank.

reviewer_1_comments: Patient is admitted for new diagnosis of CMV colitis, but was already on treatment for this (valganciclovir) prior to admission, which does not make sense. This medication would be started after diagnosis during the hospitalization. The medications are much too simplified for a post transplant patient. The labs are incomplete and the patient has a change in potassium with obvious cause or indication.
reviewer_2_comments: This case doesn’t make sense. The patient would not present with CMV colitis, that is something that would haved to be worked up and discovered (while also ruling out myriad other potential causes). The labs also don’t fit, if anything you’d expect to see an AKI and low potassium on presentation from fluid lossess and limited intake.
shared_concerns: Both reviewers found the cytomegalovirus presentation clinically incoherent.
reviewer_1_only_concerns: Valganciclovir was already a home medicine, the transplant regimen is too thin, and the recorded comment says "change in potassium with obvious cause or indication" ("unexplained" is an interpretation; the recorded wording likely intended "without"). Overall recommendation: exclude.
reviewer_2_only_concerns: The patient should not present already labeled with CMV colitis; symptoms should lead to the work-up, and volume-loss effects on kidney function and potassium should be considered. C1 is Fail. Later ratings are blank.
